stops.name: Siena: blood in the night, the little testament
stops.campa: Taken to Siena for yet more doctors, Francesco vomits blood through a whole night, and the brothers, certain the end has come, beg a word to remember him by. He cannot write; he was never able to say things at length any more; so he dictates to Brother Benedict of Piratro the three sentences that the Order calls the Siena Testament: blessing, love among brothers, fidelity to Lady Poverty and to the Church. Then, refusing to die anywhere but at Saint Mary of the Angels, he sets his face toward Assisi by way of Cortona.
stops.quote: Write that I bless all my brothers, those who are in the Order and those who will come until the end of the world. Let them always love one another; let them always love and observe our Lady holy Poverty; and let them always be faithful and subject to the prelates and all clerics of holy Mother Church.
stops.quote_source: The Siena Testament, dictated to Brother Benedict of Piratro, April 1226

stops.name: Le Celle di Cortona, the hermitage above the gorge
stops.campa: On the road home the dying man rests at the cells above Cortona, the hermitage he founded in the gorge of the torrent fifteen years before, where Brother Elias now keeps his cave. The dropsy has begun: his legs and belly swell as his sight fails. In the stone cell by the water, still shown, unchanged, narrow as a ship's berth, the tradition of Cortona holds that he set in order the thoughts that will become the great Testament. When he is carried on toward Assisi, the escort swings wide through Gubbio, for Perugia would steal a dying saint for the sake of his bones.

stops.name: Bagnara above Nocera, the knights and the begged supper
stops.campa: Against the summer heat of the plain he is carried up to Bagnara in the hills by Nocera, where the brothers have a new house among the springs. His body swells; the end is plainly near. Assisi, terrified that some other city will possess his relics, sends knights of the commune to bring him home under arms. On the road, at the poor village of Satriano, the knights can buy nothing for supper; Francesco smiles and sends them begging for the love of God, and doors that money could not open, open. The soldiers of Assisi come back fed and instructed.
stops.quote: Go and beg alms from door to door for the love of the Lord God — you found nothing for money, but for the love of God you will find everything.
stops.quote_source: Assisi Compilation 96; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 77

stops.name: Assisi, the bishop's palace and the strophe of pardon
stops.campa: Lodged under guard in the palace of the bishop, dying in the city of his birth, Francesco hears that Bishop Guido and the podestà Oportulo have excommunicated and banned each other, and that Assisi is tearing itself in two. He cannot walk to make peace, so he makes a verse: a new strophe for the Canticle, on pardon, and sends the brothers to sing it before bishop and podestà together in the cloister court. The podestà weeps and kneels; the bishop begs forgiveness and embraces him. The city is reconciled by a song: the poem doing, in his last month, the work of his whole life.
stops.quote: Praised be You, my Lord, through those who give pardon for Your love, and bear infirmity and tribulation. Blessed are those who endure in peace, for by You, Most High, they shall be crowned.
stops.quote_source: The Canticle of the Creatures, the strophe of pardon, added at Assisi, 1226 (Assisi Compilation 84)

stops.name: The road to the Porziuncola, the blessing of Assisi
stops.campa: Knowing Sister Death is at the door, he asks to be carried down to Saint Mary of the Angels, to die where the Order was born. At the crossroads by the leper-house, halfway down the plain, he asks the bearers to halt and turn the litter so that his face is toward Assisi, the city he can no longer see. He raises himself and blesses it, walls, towers and people, with the blessing the canon has kept word for word; then he is carried on down into the oak woods, and Assisi stands blessed above the plain forever.
stops.quote: Lord, as of old this city was the abode of wicked and unjust men, so now may it be the abode and dwelling of those who know You, glorify Your name, and give forth the fragrance of pure life and good renown to all Christian people. May it please You that it remain always the home of those who know and glorify Your blessed and glorious name for ever and ever. Amen.

stops.name: Porziuncola, Sister Death
stops.campa: In the infirmary hut beside the Porziuncola he adds the last strophe to the Canticle, the welcome to Sister Bodily Death, and has the brothers sing it over him. He dictates his Testament; the Lady Jacopa arrives from Rome unsummoned, forewarned from heaven, bringing the almond cakes he craved. He has bread broken and given to all in memory of the Supper, has the Passion read from John, and is laid naked on the naked earth. At dusk on Saturday, 3 October 1226, singing Psalm 141, he dies; and a great multitude of larks, birds of the light, wheel low over the hut, singing in the dark.
stops.quote: Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living man can escape. Woe to those who die in mortal sin; blessed are those whom she finds in Your most holy will, for the second death shall do them no harm. — I have done what was mine to do; may Christ teach you what is yours!
stops.quote_source: The Canticle of the Creatures, final strophe; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 214

stops.name: Assisi, San Giorgio, the burial, and the window of San Damiano
stops.campa: At dawn the whole city comes down with olive branches and torches to carry him home in triumph: the first procession of a feast the world will keep on this day forever. By his own last wish the cortege turns aside to San Damiano, and the grated window is opened so that Clare and her ladies may see him once more and kiss the wounded hands: the stigmata, hidden in life, shown openly in death. Then the city buries him at San Giorgio, where he learned his letters and first preached, until Elias's great basilica is ready, and Gregory IX, his friend Ugolino, writes him among the saints.
